lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What Food Is and Why Humans Need to Eat

pages.body:
Think about a day when you went to school without breakfast. By the middle of the morning you may have felt tired, weak and unable to concentrate. After lunch you felt better. Something in the food you ate changed how your body worked.

- What did the food give your body that it was missing earlier in the day?
- What do you think happens to a person who goes without proper food for many weeks?

Every living thing must take in food to stay alive. In this lesson we find out what food really is, which useful substances it contains, and what feeding does for the human body.

We begin by building a scientific meaning of the word food from the things your body does with it.

pages.title: What food is
pages.body:
Food is any substance that a living thing takes in to give it energy, to supply materials for growth and repair, and to provide substances that protect the body and keep its processes working properly. Rice, kenkey, fufu, beans, fish, eggs, oranges and palm oil are all foods. The useful substances inside food are called nutrients.

Next we look at the groups of nutrients, what each one does and the Ghanaian foods that supply it.

pages.title: The nutrients in food
pages.body:
| **Nutrient** | **Main work in the body** | **Common Ghanaian sources** |
|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | Supply energy for movement, thinking and keeping warm | Yam, cassava, plantain, maize, rice, bread, sugar cane |
| Proteins | Build new cells for growth and repair worn out or damaged tissues | Fish, meat, eggs, beans, groundnuts, milk |
| Fats and oils | Supply a large amount of stored energy and form a layer that keeps the body warm | Palm oil, groundnut oil, shea butter, coconut, fatty fish |
| Vitamins | Needed in small amounts to protect the body and keep organs working well | Oranges, pawpaw, mangoes, carrots, green leafy vegetables |
| Mineral salts | Build bones and teeth, make blood and help nerves and muscles work | Milk, small fish eaten with bones, green vegetables, liver |
| Water | Carries digested food and waste around the body and helps to control body temperature | Drinking water, soups, fruits such as watermelon |
| Dietary fibre | Adds bulk to food and helps the intestine to move waste out of the body | Vegetables, whole grains, beans, fruits with their skins |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What Food Is and Why Humans Need to Eat (part 3)

pages.body:
Dietary fibre is not digested and does not give energy, yet it is still part of a healthy meal because it keeps the intestine working well. A meal that contains the right amounts of all these groups is called a balanced diet.

When the body does not get enough of a nutrient over a long time, a deficiency disease can develop. The table shows some deficiency diseases that learners in Ghana should know.

| **Missing nutrient** | **Deficiency disease or sign** | **Foods that prevent it** |
|---|---|---|
| Protein | Kwashiorkor, with a swollen belly, thin limbs and poor growth in a child | Fish, eggs, beans, meat, groundnuts, milk |
| Vitamin A | Night blindness and weak eyesight | Carrots, pawpaw, mangoes, palm oil, green leafy vegetables |
| Vitamin C | Scurvy, with bleeding gums and wounds that heal slowly | Oranges, lime, guava, pawpaw, tomatoes |
| Vitamin D and calcium | Rickets, in which the bones of a child are soft and bend | Milk, small fish eaten with bones, eggs, and sunlight on the skin |
| Iron | Anaemia, with a pale look, weakness and tiredness | Liver, beans, green leafy vegetables, meat |
| Iodine | Goitre, a swelling at the front of the neck | Iodised salt and sea fish |
To see why food matters, we compare the appearance of a person who has gone without enough food for a long time with a person who eats well every day.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: A starved person compared with a well fed person

pages.title: A starved person compared with a well fed person
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Person starved for a long time** | **Person who eats well** |
|---|---|---|
| Body size | Very thin with little fat and weak muscles | Normal body mass with firm muscles |
| Skin and hair | Dry, loose skin and thin or dull hair | Smooth skin and healthy hair |
| Energy | Tires quickly and moves slowly | Active and able to work or play for long periods |
| Growth | Growth slows down or stops in a child | Child grows steadily in height and mass |
| Resistance to disease | Falls sick easily and recovers slowly | Fights infections more successfully |
| Concentration | Finds it hard to think or learn | Can concentrate and learn well |

[[pic: Two side by side drawings of a learner. One is very thin and tired from lack of food. The other is healthy and active after eating balanced meals. Label the differences in body size, skin and energy.]]

From the comparison we can now work out the jobs that feeding does for the human body.

pages.title: Deducing why feeding is important
pages.body:
- Food supplies energy so that the body can move, breathe, pump blood and think.
- Food provides materials for growth, so children and teenagers can increase in height and mass.
- Food provides materials for repair, such as healing a wound or replacing worn out cells.
- Food supplies vitamins and mineral salts that protect the body against disease.
- Food helps to keep the body at a steady temperature.
- Regular feeding keeps the brain supplied with fuel so that learners can concentrate in class.

> **Did you know?** Most people can survive for only a few days without water but for several weeks without food. This is why water is described as the most urgent need of the body after air.

questions.q: Define food in your own words.
Name the food groups that give energy and the food group that builds new cells.
State three differences between a person who has been starved for a long time and a person who eats well.
Explain why a child who is not fed properly may fall behind in class.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Alimentary Canal and What Happens to Food

pages.body:
Take a small piece of bread and chew it slowly for a full minute without swallowing. Notice how the taste changes as you chew.

- What do you notice about the taste of the bread after a minute?
- Where do you think the swallowed food goes next, and what happens to it on the way?

Food as we eat it is too large and too complex to enter the blood. It must be broken down first. In this lesson we follow a meal through the body from the mouth to the anus and see what happens in each part.

First we need to understand the process of digestion and the tube in which most of it takes place.

pages.title: Digestion and the alimentary canal
pages.body:
Digestion is the breaking down of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can pass into the blood. Some digestion is mechanical, such as chewing, which breaks food into smaller pieces. Most digestion is chemical and is done by enzymes. An enzyme is a protein made by the body that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.

The alimentary canal, also called the gut, is a long muscular tube that starts at the mouth and ends at the anus. In an adult it is about nine metres long. Food moves along it in one direction. The liver, gall bladder and pancreas are not part of the tube but they make or store juices that are poured into it, so they are called accessory organs.

[[pic: Labelled drawing of the human digestive system showing the mouth, salivary glands, oesophagus, stomach, liver, gall bladder, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.]]

We start with the mouth because digestion begins as soon as food is taken in.

pages.title: The mouth
pages.body:
The teeth cut and grind food into small pieces, which gives enzymes a larger surface to work on. The tongue rolls the chewed food into a soft ball called a bolus and pushes it to the back of the mouth for swallowing. The salivary glands make saliva, which moistens the food. Saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase, which begins to change starch into a sugar called maltose. This is why bread, boiled yam, cassava, plantain or cocoyam begins to taste slightly sweet when you chew it for a long time.

The swallowed bolus now enters a muscular tube that leads to the stomach.

pages.title: The oesophagus
pages.body:
The oesophagus, or food pipe, does not digest food. Its muscular wall squeezes behind the bolus in a wave called peristalsis, which pushes the food towards the stomach. Peristalsis happens all along the alimentary canal and works even if a person is standing on their head.

Next we look at the stomach, where food is mixed with acid and protein digestion begins.

pages.title: The stomach
pages.body:
The stomach is a stretchy muscular bag. Its walls churn the food and mix it with gastric juice. Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which kills many germs that enter with food, and an enzyme called pepsin, which begins the digestion of proteins such as egg, meat and fish. Mucus covers the stomach wall and protects it from the acid. After a few hours the food has become a thick, creamy liquid called chyme, which is released in small amounts into the small intestine. Starchy foods such as yam and bread continue to be digested by the saliva they carry for a while, but the acid soon stops that enzyme from working.

The small intestine is where most digestion is completed and where nearly all digested food is absorbed.

pages.title: The small intestine
pages.body: The small intestine is a narrow tube about six metres long. It is called small only because it is narrow, not because it is short. The first part, the duodenum, receives bile from the liver and gall bladder and pancreatic juice from the pancreas. Bile does not contain an enzyme. It breaks large fat droplets into tiny droplets, which is called emulsification, so that the enzyme lipase can digest fats and oils such as palm oil more quickly. Pancreatic juice contains enzymes that digest starch, protein and fats. The wall of the small intestine adds its own juice, which completes the job. Digestion of a meal that contains starch, protein and oil is complete by the end of the small intestine.
Finally we follow the undigested waste to the end of the canal.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The large intestine, rectum and anus

pages.title: The large intestine, rectum and anus
pages.body: The large intestine is wider but shorter than the small intestine, about one and a half metres long. It absorbs most of the remaining water and some mineral salts from the waste. What is left, mainly fibre, dead cells and bacteria, forms solid faeces. The faeces are stored in the rectum and pushed out through the anus when a person goes to the toilet.

| **Part of the canal** | **Main action on food** |
|---|---|
| Mouth | Chewing, mixing with saliva and the start of starch digestion |
| Oesophagus | Pushes food to the stomach by peristalsis |
| Stomach | Churning, killing germs with acid and the start of protein digestion |
| Small intestine | Completes digestion of starch, protein and fats and absorbs digested food |
| Large intestine | Absorbs water and mineral salts and forms faeces |
| Rectum and anus | Store faeces and remove them from the body |

Now we put together the enzymes that work along the canal, because each enzyme digests one kind of food and makes one kind of product.

pages.title: The enzymes of digestion
pages.body:
| **Where it is made** | **Enzyme** | **Food it acts on** | **Product** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Salivary glands | Salivary amylase | Starch | Maltose |
| Wall of the stomach | Pepsin | Protein | Short chains of amino acids called peptides |
| Pancreas | Pancreatic amylase | Starch | Maltose |
| Pancreas | Trypsin | Protein | Peptides |
| Pancreas and wall of the small intestine | Lipase | Fats and oils | Fatty acids and glycerol |
| Wall of the small intestine | Maltase | Maltose | Glucose |
| Wall of the small intestine | Peptidases | Peptides | Amino acids |

Bile is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is not an enzyme. It is a green fluid that emulsifies fats and also makes the contents of the small intestine slightly alkaline, which is the condition in which the enzymes of the small intestine work best.

Each enzyme works on only one kind of food. Amylase digests starch but cannot digest protein. Enzymes work best at body temperature, about 37 degrees Celsius, and each one needs the right acid or alkaline condition. Pepsin works in the acid of the stomach, while the enzymes of the small intestine work in a slightly alkaline liquid. Putting the table together gives the full path of each food.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Following some foods through the body

pages.body:
- Starch is changed to maltose by amylase in the mouth and the small intestine, and maltose is changed to glucose by maltase.
- Protein is changed to peptides by pepsin in the stomach and by trypsin in the small intestine, and peptides are changed to amino acids by peptidases.
- Fats and oils are emulsified by bile and then changed to fatty acids and glycerol by lipase.

To finish, we trace a few familiar foods to see how the same canal handles different nutrients.

pages.title: Following some foods through the body
pages.body:
- Boiled yam, cassava, plantain and cocoyam are rich in starch. Digestion of starch begins in the mouth and is completed in the small intestine.
- Egg and meat are rich in protein. Digestion begins in the stomach and ends in the small intestine.
- Palm oil is a fat. It is not digested in the mouth or the stomach. Bile and enzymes in the small intestine digest it.
- An orange has mainly water, simple sugars and vitamin C. These are small and soluble, so very little digestion is needed before absorption.

questions.q: Define digestion and state the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion.
Name the parts of the alimentary canal in the order that food passes through them.
State two jobs of the stomach.
Explain why bile is needed for the digestion of palm oil even though bile contains no enzyme.
Name the enzyme that acts on each of starch, protein and fats and oils in the small intestine and state the product of each.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: End Products of Digestion, Absorption and Food Tests

pages.body:
A bowl of fufu and groundnut soup contains starch, protein and oil. After a few hours the large pieces of food have disappeared from your gut, yet your blood has not become thick with fufu.

- What do you think the large food molecules are changed into?
- How do you think these changed substances get from the gut into the blood?

In the last lesson we followed food through the gut. Here we find out what each type of food is finally changed into, how those products enter the body, and how we can test foods in the laboratory to find out which nutrients they contain.

We start with the small molecules that remain after enzymes have finished their work.

pages.title: End products of digestion
pages.body:
- Starch is digested to sugar. Starch is first changed to maltose and then to glucose.
- Protein is digested to amino acids.
- Fats and oils are digested to fatty acids and glycerol.

[[pic: Flow chart with three rows. Starch to maltose to glucose. Protein to amino acids. Fats and oils to fatty acids and glycerol. Label the enzymes amylase, protease and lipase on the arrows.]]

Glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol are small and soluble. They are small enough to pass through the wall of the small intestine, which large starch, protein and fat molecules could never do.

Now we look at how the lining of the small intestine takes in these small molecules.

pages.title: How digested food is absorbed
pages.body: Absorption is the movement of digested food from the gut into the blood or lymph. It happens mainly in the small intestine. The inside wall of the small intestine is covered with millions of tiny finger shaped projections called villi. Each villus has a wall only one cell thick and contains a network of blood capillaries and a lymph vessel called a lacteal. The villi greatly increase the surface area for absorption, and the thin wall and rich blood supply make absorption fast.

- Glucose and amino acids pass into the blood capillaries of the villi. The blood carries them to the liver and then to all the cells of the body.
- Fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lacteals and are carried in the lymph, which later joins the blood.
- Water and mineral salts are absorbed in the small intestine and the large intestine.

The villi are well suited to their work for four reasons.

- They are very many and covered with even smaller projections, so the surface area for absorption is very large.
- The wall of each villus is only one cell thick, so digested food has a very short distance to travel.
- Each villus has a network of blood capillaries, so absorbed glucose and amino acids are carried away quickly, which keeps the movement into the blood going.
- Each villus has a lacteal that takes in fatty acids and glycerol.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Importance of the end products to the body

pages.body:
Cells then use the absorbed nutrients. Glucose is used to release energy, amino acids are used to build new proteins for growth and repair, and fatty acids and glycerol are used as an energy store and to build cell membranes. This use of absorbed food by the cells is called assimilation.

[[pic: Enlarged drawing of one villus showing the thin wall, a blood capillary and a lacteal, with arrows showing glucose and amino acids entering the capillary and fatty acids entering the lacteal.]]

Next we see why the body needs each end product after it has been absorbed.

pages.title: Importance of the end products to the body
pages.body:
| **End product** | **Importance in the human body** |
|---|---|
| Glucose | It is broken down in the cells during respiration to release energy for movement, growth, thinking and keeping the body warm. Brain cells depend on a steady supply of glucose. |
| Amino acids | They are joined together to make new proteins for growth and for repairing worn out or damaged tissues. They are also used to make enzymes, some hormones and the antibodies that fight disease. |
| Fatty acids and glycerol | They release a large amount of energy, more than the same mass of glucose. They are used to build cell membranes, to store energy, to form a layer under the skin that keeps the body warm and to cushion organs such as the kidneys. |
The body does not always use all the digested food at once, so we now follow the extra amounts.

pages.title: What happens to excess products
pages.body:
| **End product** | **What happens to the excess** | **Effect on the body** |
|---|---|---|
| Glucose | The liver and muscles change some glucose into glycogen and store it. When blood sugar falls between meals the liver changes glycogen back to glucose. The stores are small, so any further excess is changed into fat and stored. | A person who eats more energy food than the body uses gains mass and may become overweight. |
| Amino acids | Amino acids cannot be stored. The liver removes the nitrogen part in a process called deamination and changes it into urea. Blood carries urea to the kidneys and it leaves the body in urine. The rest of the amino acid is used to release energy or changed to fat. | This is why a person who eats too much protein passes more urea in the urine. |
| Fatty acids and glycerol | The excess is stored as fat in fatty tissue under the skin and around organs. The body uses this fat for energy when food is short. | Too much stored fat can lead to obesity, which raises the risk of heart disease. |
Finally we learn four simple tests that show whether a food sample contains starch, glucose, protein or fats and oils.

pages.title: Practical tests on food
pages.body:
| **Nutrient** | **Test** | **Positive result** |
|---|---|---|
| Starch | Add a few drops of iodine solution to the food sample | Colour changes from orange brown to blue black |
| Glucose | Add Benedict solution to a little of the food in water and heat in a hot water bath for a few minutes | Blue changes to green, yellow, orange or brick red depending on the amount of glucose |
| Protein | Add sodium hydroxide solution and then a few drops of dilute copper sulphate solution | Colour changes from blue to violet or purple |
| Fats and oils | Rub the food on brown paper and hold it to the light | A clear oily mark that does not dry away |

Boiled yam or cassava gives a positive result for starch. Orange juice gives a positive result for glucose. Egg white gives a positive result for protein. Groundnuts and palm oil leave a clear mark on brown paper. A food that gives no colour change is said to give a negative result for that test.

> **Safety** Iodine stains the skin and clothes. Sodium hydroxide and copper sulphate solutions can harm the skin and eyes, so your teacher must handle them and you must wear goggles. Heat the Benedict test in a hot water bath, never by holding the test tube in a flame. Never taste any food used in a laboratory test.
> **Did you know?** The small intestine is called small because it is narrow. It is actually the longest part of the alimentary canal and the part where most absorption happens.

questions.q: State the end product of digestion of starch, of protein and of fats and oils.
Describe two features of a villus that make absorption fast.
Write down the test and the positive result for starch.
Explain why large molecules such as starch must be digested before they can be absorbed.
Describe what happens to excess glucose and to excess amino acids in the body.
State the importance of glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids and glycerol in the body.

pages.body:
- Food is a substance taken in to supply energy, materials for growth and repair, and substances for protection and regulation. The useful parts of food are called nutrients.
- The nutrient groups are carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins, mineral salts and water, with dietary fibre helping the gut to work well.
- A person who is starved appears thin, weak and unwell compared with a person who eats well. This shows why feeding is important for energy, growth, repair and protection.
- The alimentary canal runs from the mouth through the oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and rectum to the anus. The liver, gall bladder and pancreas are accessory organs.
- Digestion begins in the mouth with starch, continues in the stomach with protein and is completed in the small intestine.
- Each enzyme digests one kind of food. Amylase digests starch to maltose, maltase changes maltose to glucose, pepsin and trypsin digest protein to peptides, peptidases change peptides to amino acids, and lipase digests fats and oils to fatty acids and glycerol. Bile emulsifies fats but is not an enzyme.
- End products are glucose from starch, amino acids from protein, and fatty acids and glycerol from fats and oils.
- Villi in the small intestine have a large surface area, a wall one cell thick, blood capillaries and a lacteal, so they absorb digested food quickly into the blood and lymph.
- Glucose supplies energy, amino acids build and repair tissues and make enzymes and antibodies, and fatty acids and glycerol supply energy, form cell membranes and keep the body warm.
- Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles and then as fat. Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver to make urea, which leaves in urine. Excess fats are stored under the skin and around organs.
- A lack of a nutrient causes a deficiency disease such as kwashiorkor, scurvy, rickets, anaemia or goitre.
- Iodine, Benedict solution, sodium hydroxide with copper sulphate, and brown paper are used to test for starch, glucose, protein and fats and oils.
